deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematical derivation. It is a qualitative physiological-mechanical passage from Riemann's fragment on the mechanics of the ear ('Mechanik des Ohres'), posthumously published in 1867 by Henle in the Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin.

Content, step by step:
(1) The sentence carried over from the previous page continues. The previous page proposed separating the 'listening' ear (lauschendes Ohr, adapted for precise hearing) from the non-listening ear. For certain questions one should also distinguish the ear of the newborn from that of the adult.
(2) Definition. The ear is 'listening' when the tensor tympani muscle pulls the stapes footplate slightly against (into) the labyrinth fluid. The pressure in the labyrinth fluid then slightly exceeds the pressure of the air in the tympanic cavity. In modern terms (my notation): p_lab - p_air = F/A > 0, where F is the net inward force transmitted to the footplate and A is the footplate area.
(3) Consequence. Through this small preload, the solid parts whose contact must be secured (the ossicular joint surfaces: malleus-incus, incus-stapes) are pressed slightly against each other. This removes play or looseness in the chain.
(4) Concession to sceptics. Some readers may find such a continual tension of the apparatus (the tympanic membrane perhaps excepted) improbable. They may assume instead that, under temperature changes, the ossicles change position through the action of the suspensory and joint ligaments and the gradual change of muscle contraction, without being pressed against each other.
(5) Reason given. The clause 'because we have found ...' continues on the next page: '... that only then is the exact interlocking of all parts of the apparatus secured.' This explains why Riemann ties the precisely working, listening ear to the preloaded state. The next page concludes that his analysis then holds at least for the deliberately adapted, listening ear.

The underlying mechanical idea is that a small static preload keeps a chain of articulated rigid bodies in contact, so that small oscillations are transmitted without slack. No equations are written on the page.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. The logical link of the 'weil' clause (step 5) is somewhat elliptic: it justifies why the preloaded state is the one relevant to precise hearing, not the sceptics' alternative. This is a stylistic looseness, not an error.

results.what: Hypothesis that in the attentive ('listening') ear the tensor tympani applies a small static preload. The stapes footplate is pushed into the perilymph, labyrinth pressure slightly exceeds tympanic air pressure, and the ossicular joints are held in firm contact.
results.modern_name: Static preload / tensor tympani accommodation hypothesis; ossicular chain coupling under muscle tension
results.usually_credited_to: Ideas on accommodation of the middle-ear muscles circulated in mid-19th-century physiology (Johannes Müller, Toynbee, Politzer, later Helmholtz 1868 'Die Mechanik der Gehörknöchelchen und des Trommelfells')

results.what: Methodological distinction between the listening/non-listening ear and between newborn and adult ear.
results.modern_name: Distinction of physiological states of the middle ear

deep.surprise_reason: The passage is part of Riemann's known and published (1867) fragment on the mechanics of the ear. It is purely qualitative, with no mathematics and nothing beyond what the published text contains.

checkable.sympy: F, A = symbols('F A', positive=True); dp = F/A; simplify(dp > 0)
checkable.asserts: Trivial static balance on the stapes footplate: a positive inward force F over area A gives labyrinth pressure exceeding tympanic air pressure (p_lab - p_air = F/A > 0). This is the only quantitative content implicit on the page.
